newsitem.title: CHINA: France puts aside human rights for China deals.
newsitem.headline: France puts aside human rights for China deals.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac's four-day China visit, which ended on Sunday, showed France was prepared to put business before human rights principles to win new contracts with the emerging world power, analysts said.

During the trip, the first state visit to China by a French leader for 14 years, Chirac signed an agreement with Chinese President Jiang Zemin to develop bilateral economic and political ties into the 21st century.
The trip also saw the signing of $1.8 billion in deals, including a $1.5 billion accord for European consortium Airbus Industrie to sell 30 passenger jets to Chinese airlines.

Analysts say the deals at least indirectly stemmed from France's decision last month not to back a motion in the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva criticising China's human rights record.
"France was the first of the European Union countries to jump ship in Geneva," said a Western diplomat.
Chirac's message on the purpose of his trip was clear -- France does not want to be left behind in participating in China's economic boom.

"Thanks to the fantastic way its economy has taken off China is already one of the major world powers," he said in a speech in Shanghai where he opened a major French trade exhibition. "In one or two generations you (China) will be at the very top."
"France is delighted that your country should be taking its rightful place on the world scene," Chirac said. "We would like to accompany you in this historical process."
"It's not as if the French don't care at all about human rights," said another Western diplomat. "They just made a conclusion that some other countries did as well."

Relations between France and China soured in the early 1990s over France's sales of jet fighters to China's rival Taiwan and French criticism of Beijing's crackdown on the 1989 student-led democracy movement.

These issues have now been pushed aside. Chirac said in Beijing that France would not sell any more armaments to Taiwan, and that the two countries had agreed to disagree on definitions of human rights.

On Saturday, he told Chinese officials and representatives from more than 300 French companies participating in a high-tech exhibition that he would lend government support to boost his country's exports to and investment in China.
Business deals in China will also help Chirac at home, where his centre-right political coalition is facing two-round May 25-June 1 parliamentary elections, analysts said.
"The feeling is a successful visit to China will allow him to be a successful statesman on the world stage," said one diplomat.

Amongst other deals agreed during the visit, Airbus signed a contract with Aviation Industies of China, Alenia of Italy's Finmeccanica and Singapore Technologies Aerospace to build a 100-seater commercial jetliner.
France's Rhone-Poulenc also signed a 500 million franc ($88 million) joint venture to produce pesticide in China.
